title: The Creed and the prayers of the faithful
hook: the whole church says what it believes, then prays for the world

segments.voice: Yesterday, the homily, a conversation that opens the readings. Your line was the word, for today. Which sentence did you keep? Day one hundred and eleven.

The year is 325, in a lakeside town called Nicaea, in what is now Turkey. About three hundred bishops have traveled there, some of them with scars from the persecutions only a few years before. One bishop is missing an eye. Another has crippled hands. The emperor himself has called the meeting, because the Church is tearing itself apart over one question: is Jesus fully God, or is he the first and greatest thing God made? What they decided that summer is still said out loud, every Sunday, by Catholics around the world and many other Christians too. Today: the Nicene Creed.

A priest in Alexandria named Arius had been teaching that the Son was created by the Father, glorious, but made. His followers even sang it: there was a time when he was not. The council said no. To pin it down, they reached for a Greek word: homoousios, of the same substance, the same being as the Father. In today's English Mass the word is consubstantial. Not a lesser god. Not a creature. God from God, light from light. A second council, at Constantinople in 381, added more about the Holy Spirit, and that longer creed is the one said at Mass today, right after the homily. You learned the shorter Apostles' Creed ten days ago. This one is its bigger sibling, built for an argument. One honest detail. Centuries later, churches in the West added a phrase saying the Spirit comes from the Father and the Son. In Latin, filioque. Orthodox Christians never accepted that addition, and it remains one of the questions between the churches. Many Eastern Catholics say the creed without it. Then, straight after the creed, the Mass turns outward. The prayers of the faithful. Someone reads short intentions: for the Church, for leaders of nations, for people who are suffering, for the sick and the dead of this parish. After each, everyone answers together, asking God to hear. Paul asked for this, in the Douay-Rheims: "that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all men." First the church says what it believes. Then, believing it, the church asks.
screen: `THERE WAS A TIME WHEN HE WAS NOT?` · `HOMOOUSIOS: THE SAME BEING.` · `THE FILIOQUE, EAST AND WEST.` · `THEN PRAYERS FOR THE WORLD.` · then, large: `SUPPLICATIONS, PRAYERS, INTERCESSIONS, AND THANKSGIVINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one need in the news. Settle, and breathe. Think of one headline from this week. A flood, a war, a sick child in your town, a family who lost their home. Don't scroll for it. Pick the first one that comes. Picture the people inside it, not the numbers. If you pray, you can hold them up now, the way a parish does after the creed. If you don't, hold them in your attention, and wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Nicene Creed. The statement of faith from the councils of Nicaea and Constantinople, said at Sunday Mass: God from God, light from light. Today's word.
Your line: we believe, then we ask. Today, when you hear about someone in trouble, don't just scroll past. Stop, and ask on their behalf, in whatever way is yours. Day one hundred and eleven.

howItsDone: At Sunday Mass the congregation stands after the homily to profess the Nicene Creed, bowing at the words about the incarnation; then a deacon or reader announces the universal prayer, or prayers of the faithful, and the people respond to each intention.

fork.setup: you're a bishop at Nicaea in 325. Arius says the Son was created, the greatest of God's works. what does the council say?
options: the Son is created, but greater than angels.
the Son is of the same being as the Father.

fork.reveal: they chose homoousios: of the same being as the Father. in today's English Mass, consubstantial. God from God, light from light.

original.note: Greek: of the same being, the council of Nicaea's word for the Son's relation to the Father.

trapdoor: what you thought: a long list said standing up.
what it means: a statement hammered out in a crisis over who Jesus is, followed at once by prayers for the world.
what a scholar hears: the Niceno-Constantinopolitan creed of 381, homoousios, and the filioque, added in the West and still unresolved with the Orthodox.

sources.ref: Creed of Nicaea (325) and Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed (381)
General Instruction of the Roman Missal 67–71

notes: Douay-Rheims 1 Timothy 2:1 fragment given from memory; confirm.

Nicaea: traditionally 318 bishops; 'about three hundred' used. Scarred confessors (e.g. Paphnutius, one eye; Paul of Neocaesarea, crippled hands) are reported by early historians (Theodoret, Socrates); confirm.
Arian slogan 'there was a time when he was not' (ēn pote hote ouk ēn): given as their teaching; confirm.
'God from God, light from light' is traditional creed wording, also in ICEL; short and traditional, spoken without quotation marks. Confirm acceptable.
Filioque described without ranking (CCC 246–248 discusses it). Many Eastern Catholic churches omit it; confirm phrasing 'many'.

'A billion Catholics': the Catholic Church reports about 1.4 billion members; not all attend weekly. Reviewer softened the hook to 'Catholics around the world'. Also note the creed said today is the 381 form, not exactly what Nicaea decided in 325; the hook's 'what they decided that summer is still said' is a simplification the teach corrects.
